opus-5.5.text:
Well, the starting point is to look at what's wrong with the standard model of AI, which is the model we've been using since the field began. We build machines that optimize a fixed objective that we supply. That works fine when the machine is not very capable and operates in a small, well-defined world, like a chessboard. But as systems become more capable and act in the real world, it becomes a recipe for disaster. We simply don't know how to write down our objectives completely and correctly. This is the King Midas problem: you get exactly what you asked for, not what you actually wanted. And a sufficiently capable system pursuing a mis-specified objective will resist our attempts to correct it, because being corrected or switched off interferes with achieving the objective it was given.

So the alternative is to build machines whose only goal is to satisfy human preferences, but which *know they don't know* what those preferences are. That uncertainty turns out to be the key. A machine that is certain about its objective has no reason to defer to us. It treats our interventions as obstacles. A machine that is uncertain has every reason to defer. It will ask permission before doing something drastic, because it's not sure we'd approve. It will act cautiously in areas where it doesn't understand our preferences. And, most importantly, it will allow itself to be switched off. If a human goes to switch it off, that's evidence that whatever the machine was about to do is something the human doesn't want. Since the machine wants to avoid doing what we don't want, it's happy to be switched off. We showed this formally in the off-switch game: the incentive to allow shutdown follows directly from the uncertainty about the objective. As the uncertainty goes to zero, that incentive disappears.

The other thing I like about this framing is that it gives you a concrete technical research program rather than just a slogan. You can formalize it as an assistance game: a game with at least two players, a human and a machine. The human has preferences, and the machine is designed to help the human but doesn't observe those preferences directly. It has to learn them from human behavior, from choices, from what we say, from the way the world has been arranged by people who had those preferences. This connects to inverse reinforcement learning, but it's richer than that, because both parties know they're in this situation. The human has an incentive to teach and the machine has an incentive to ask, to defer, to observe. You get behaviors like explanation and clarification emerging from the structure of the problem itself, rather than having to be bolted on.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. There are enormous open problems. Humans are not rational, so the machine can't just read our preferences straight off our behavior. It has to understand the cognitive limitations and the emotional and cultural processes that generate what we do. There are many humans, not one, so you inherit all the problems of moral philosophy and social choice theory about how to aggregate preferences and make trade-offs between people. Preferences themselves change over time, and the machine could in principle manipulate them, which is a real worry. And I'd point out that today's large language models don't fit this framework at all. We don't really know what objectives, if any, they've absorbed, and we certainly can't say they're uncertain in the right way about human preferences. That's one reason I'm concerned about how the field is developing.

But as a foundation, I think it's the right one. It replaces the idea of machines that are intelligent to the extent that they achieve *their* objectives with machines that are beneficial to the extent that they achieve *our* objectives. Once you make that shift, uncertainty isn't a bug to be engineered away. It's the thing that keeps humans in control.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the standard fixed-objective model with an uncertainty-based alternative, but does not characterize that alternative as a generalization of frameworks with exactly known objectives.

r003.rationale: It describes the machine learning preferences from human behavior and says it has an incentive to ask and observe.

r005.rationale: It connects uncertainty to deference and says a shutdown attempt is evidence of human preferences, but does not clearly state that human commands generally serve as new evidence about those preferences.

r006.rationale: It says the machine is happy to be switched off when a human tries to shut it down, because that indicates the human does not want its planned action.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the standard model of AI, the one we've worked with since the beginning of the field, says that you build a machine that optimizes a fixed objective, and the human's job is to specify that objective correctly. And the trouble is that we're not very good at specifying objectives. If you leave anything out, the machine will treat the omitted things as having zero value, and it will happily sacrifice them to squeeze out a little more of whatever you did write down. That's the King Midas problem. Midas got exactly what he asked for, and it was a catastrophe.

Now, as long as machines are not very capable, this doesn't matter much. If you get the objective wrong, the machine makes a mess, you switch it off, you try again. But as systems become more capable, two things happen. First, the consequences of a misspecified objective become much larger, because the machine is more effective at pursuing it. And second, a machine that is certain about its objective has a very strong reason not to let you switch it off, because being switched off means it fails to achieve the objective. So you get this perverse situation where a more intelligent machine is harder to correct.

The idea behind uncertainty is to reverse that logic. Instead of giving the machine a fixed objective, you build it so that its only goal is to further human preferences, but it knows that it doesn't know what those preferences are. It has to learn them, from our behavior, from what we say, from what we do and don't object to. And once you set things up that way, something quite nice falls out mathematically. If a human tries to switch the machine off, the machine reasons: the human is trying to switch me off, and the human knows things about their own preferences that I don't, so this is probably because what I'm doing is not what they want. Therefore, letting myself be switched off is the right thing to do. The machine has a positive incentive to defer to us, precisely because it's uncertain.

So it's not that uncertainty is some vague virtue, like humility. It's that uncertainty about the objective is what makes deference, corrigibility, asking permission, all of those behaviors, actually rational for the machine rather than things we have to bolt on and hope it doesn't find a way around. And I think that gives us a foundation where more capable systems are safer rather than more dangerous, which is what we need if we're going to keep building them.

r001.rationale: It says the machine’s goal is to further human preferences while also knowing it does not know what those preferences are.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the standard fixed-objective model with an approach that represents uncertainty about the objective.

r003.rationale: It says the machine must learn human preferences from behavior, speech, and what people do or do not object to.

r004.rationale: It describes learning, deference, and permission-seeking, but does not state that objective uncertainty creates an incentive to act cautiously toward the world.

r005.rationale: It treats a human’s attempt to switch the machine off as evidence about preferences, but does not explain deference to human commands generally as a response to new evidence.

r006.rationale: It says that when a human tries to switch the machine off, the machine can reason that allowing itself to be switched off is the right action.

astra-6.text:
Well, the problem with the standard model of AI is that we give the machine an objective, and then we ask it to achieve that objective as well as possible. If the objective leaves out something we care about—which it almost certainly will—then greater competence can actually make the outcome worse. The machine has no reason to regard our objections as evidence that its objective is wrong.

So the alternative is to say: the machine’s purpose is to help humans achieve what they want, but it doesn’t know exactly what that is. That uncertainty is crucial. It gives the machine a reason to ask questions, to learn from human choices, and to be cautious about actions whose consequences we might dislike.

It also changes the logic of being switched off. A machine with a fixed objective may resist shutdown because it can’t achieve that objective if it’s switched off. A machine that’s uncertain about human preferences can interpret our wish to switch it off as evidence that it’s doing something undesirable. So allowing itself to be switched off can serve its purpose, rather than frustrate it.

Now, uncertainty alone isn’t a complete solution. Human behavior is complicated, and there are many humans with conflicting preferences. But it gives us a foundation in which deference to people follows from the machine’s purpose, rather than being a constraint we bolt onto an otherwise single-minded optimizer.

r001.rationale: The response says the machine’s purpose is to help humans achieve what they want while acknowledging that it does not know exactly what they want.

r002.rationale: It presents uncertainty as an alternative to the standard fixed-objective model, but does not characterize it as a generalization of frameworks that assume known objectives.

r003.rationale: It says uncertainty gives the machine a reason to ask questions and learn from human choices.

r004.rationale: It says uncertainty gives the machine a reason to be cautious about actions whose consequences humans might dislike.

r005.rationale: It treats a shutdown request as evidence of an undesirable outcome, but does not explain deference to human commands generally as a response to new evidence about preferences.

r006.rationale: It says a machine uncertain about human preferences can take a wish to switch it off as evidence and allow shutdown in service of its purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic problem is that if you give a machine a fixed objective, then its job is to achieve that objective, whether or not you actually like the consequences. And we’re very unlikely to specify everything we care about correctly. You can’t simply say, “Oh, and be careful,” and expect that to cover all the things we left out.

So the alternative is to say that the machine’s purpose is to help humans achieve their objectives, but it doesn’t know exactly what those objectives are. That uncertainty is crucial. It gives the machine a reason to ask questions, to learn from human behavior, and to be cautious about actions whose consequences we might dislike.

It also changes the incentives around human control. If the machine is certain about its objective, being switched off prevents it from achieving that objective, so it has a reason to resist. If it’s uncertain, then our wish to switch it off is evidence that it may be doing something we don’t want. It has a reason to defer to us.

That doesn’t solve every problem. Human behavior is complicated, and we have conflicting preferences. But it gives us a foundation where assistance and deference can follow from the system’s purpose, rather than being extra rules we hope will hold up.

r002.rationale: It contrasts fixed objectives with uncertainty, but does not characterize uncertainty as a generalization of frameworks that assume exactly known objectives.

r005.rationale: It explains that a human’s wish to switch the machine off is evidence it may be doing something unwanted, giving it reason to defer.
